method: Track each horse through consecutive starts within 365 days.
Promotion is defined as moving to a strictly higher mapped class.
Primary race-level comparison requires the same surface and exact distance; race-pair duplicates are removed.
Strict sensitivity comparison additionally requires same venue, course division and going.
Race-level clock is the winning time; field median time is also checked so the result is not winner-only.
Same-class repeat starts are used as a control for natural race-to-race drift.
interpretation: The race-level clock clearly becomes faster when the same horse steps into a higher class, even when surface and distance are held fixed; the strict same-venue/course/going check points the same way.
The field median time improves almost as much as the winner time, so this is not merely one exceptional winner producing the effect.
For 3-win to open, a universal +0.2-second class correction is not directly supported as an exact constant: the observed race-level shift is closer to 0.3-0.45 seconds in these matched comparisons.

However, the promoted horse's own realized time does not automatically get faster; in strict 3-win to open matches it is on average 0.305 seconds slower because the horse loses more ground to a faster race.
Therefore a class correction should be modeled as a race-environment / latent-output adjustment, not as a mechanical subtraction from every horse's future finishing time.
The precise value of a published '+0.2 sec' formula cannot be validated without the formula's exact target definition.
